newsitem.title: USA: N. Carolina voting ensures steady new issue supply.
newsitem.headline: N. Carolina voting ensures steady new issue supply.

text.p: This week's election will create a steady suppply of new municipal issues from North Carolina, deputy treasurer Everett Chalk said Wednesday.

In addition to $1.8 billion of state general obligation bonds for schools, and $950 million of state GOs for roads, North Carolina voters approved $311.76 million of local GO issues, said Chalk, who oversees the state's local bond deals.
"We anticipate that we'll be coming to market with a sizeable amount of bonds here pretty soon," Chalk said.

The only GO referendum to fail in the entire state was a $2 million Greensboro issue to finance improvements at the baseball stadium used by the Greensboro Bats minor league team, Chalk said. Even there, voters approved five other GO bonds totalling $35 million.
"It is unusual that you would have that many that passed at one time," Chalk said.

Even more surprising, he said, "We had quite a few parks and recreation bonds," which tend to have a higher failure rate than those for police, schools and other projects more likely to be considered essential government services.

Both of the statewide issues are bigger than any previously approved in North Carolina. And both passed by large margins. The school proposal passed with 165,027 votes for and 41,807 against. The highway bonds passed with 129,142 votes for and 74,671 against, preliminary totals show.

The statewide bonds are to be issued incrementally over the next four years. Authorizations for the local issues are good for seven years, though most are expected to come to market much sooner than that.

Additionally, Chalk said, $1.5 billion of local bonds had previously been authorized but not yet issued. Together, that will provide an unusual flow of new issues in a highly rated state where traders complain of a chronic shortage of bonds.
"We are going to keep a close eye on it. We like a steady supply in the market place. In some years past, it's been a feast or famine situation," Chalk said.
